III. IMPACT OF THE PROPOSED ACTION
Introduction: Secretarial authority to carry out a program to restore populations of endangered animals already exists in the Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1969. The proposed action constitutes an increment to present authority. The legislation, for the most part, does not change the basic action—preserving and restoring endangered species, but it strengthens the means of the Federal Government to carry out that action. Most impacts discussed herein, are impacts of degree and change the impact of the action under present authority only in terms of time or the efficiency of the steps that would be used under the present authority. For example, the plan of action for restoration of species "X" is not appreciably changed under the proposed legislation, but goals may be accomplished sooner and may, in some cases, cost less than under present authority. Because more species will come under provisions of the legislation, the total impact of species preservation will be multiplied over what it is now.
This discussion is intended to draw attention to incremental impacts, or those impacts for which the proposed legislation would be responsible. However, it is impossible to discuss increments without also discussing impacts of the action under present authority. Therefore, this section of the statement will constitute a review of the impacts accumulated through all authority culminating in the proposed Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1973.
Impacts of the proposed action will occur in five general areas: (1) impacts on the animals themselves that are subject to provisions of the proposed legislation as well as associated species; (2) economic impact; (3) impacts on people and society; (4) research impacts; and (5) political impacts.
